who: People reading in a second language
takeaways: There is a way to find the expanded form or meaning of abbreviations, including acronyms like APR, KYC or SLA.
Abbreviations save space but assume knowledge. Some readers do not know them, and a screen reader may read them as strange words.
This is Level AAA. You can meet it by writing the full form the first time it appears, linking to a glossary, or giving a definition people can open.
Designers own where the full form fits: in the label, the helper text, or a definition people can reach by keyboard and touch.
failures: A pricing table full of acronyms with no key
Status chips like “PND” and “ACK” with no explanation
Expansions shown only in a hover tooltip
check: Search your copy and labels for abbreviations and acronyms, including status codes.
For each, find the full form on the same screen or one step away.
Make sure the expansion can be reached without a mouse.

quiz.question: A loan comparison card shows “APR 7.9%”. Space is tight. What meets 3.1.4?
options: Leave it. APR is a standard term
Show the full form only in the page’s source code
Add a visible explanation on first use, “Annual percentage rate (APR)”, or a definition people can open
quiz.why: Standard to the industry is not standard to every reader. A full form on first use or an openable definition reaches everyone, including keyboard and touch users.

spec: List each abbreviation with its full form and plain meaning.
Mark where the full form is shown, and how a definition opens if it is not visible.
Note any abbreviation that screen readers should hear spelled out, such as letters instead of a word.
review: Which abbreviations here would a first-time customer not know?
Is this abbreviation saving real space, or just habit?
Where can someone find out what this stands for?
tradeoff: Full forms make tight UI like chips and tables longer. Use the full form where space allows, and keep a short form with an easy way to expand it where it does not.
system: Keep a shared list of approved abbreviations with their expansions, and give chips and table headers an optional definition slot.
pitch: Acronyms are insider language. Explaining them once makes our product feel open to newcomers.
